https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/books.text: Subscriber Only Books Review Herta Müller’s The Village on the Edge of the World: Survival under Ceausescu’s regime A book about language, memory and the imagination’s resistance to fear A strident Nicolae Ceausescu at the party congress on November 24th, 1989. Photograph: Gerard Fouet/AFP/Getty Images Adam Wyeth Sat Jul 25 2026 - 04:16 • 2 MIN READ The Village on the Edge of the World: Writing and Surviving Ceaușescu’s Romania Author : Herta Müller, translated by Kate McNaughton ISBN-13 : 9781783788170 Publisher : Granta Guideline Price : £16.99; 256pp There are writers who bear witness to history, and there are writers who alter the way we see it. Herta Müller belongs to the latter category. The Village on the Edge of the World is presented as a series of conversations about her life and work, yet it reads more like a memoir of survival under Ceausescu’s dictatorship, a book about language, memory and the imagination’s resistance to fear. It becomes something rarer than autobiography: a defence of literature itself. Müller grew up in the Banat village of Nițchidorf, “as small as a thimble on the edge of the world”, a place shadowed by both fascism and communism. Her father had served in the Waffen-SS; her mother survived deportation to a Soviet labour camp. Müller repeatedly returns to Romania’s failure to confront its complicity in nazism and wartime atrocities. The village is not a lost paradise but a psychic landscape where unspoken histories have seeped into language, objects and silence. Müller shows that totalitarianism is not merely political but perceptual. The damage done to language, memory and the inner life. She writes vividly about interrogations, informers and the Securitate’s petty cruelties, including the fox fur in her apartment repeatedly mutilated to signal that she was being watched. Under dictatorship, speech becomes contaminated by fear, and the writer must find new ways of seeing and saying. The result is prose of extraordinary descriptive intensity, where the ordinary world becomes unsettling, lyrical and revelatory. READ MORE Dara McAnulty on Wainwright Prize shortlist Kitten by Stacey Yu: Strange, vibrant and genuinely idiosyncratic novel The Quickening by Claire McGowan: A powerful novel of motherhood, cowardice and courage Flirting with Evil – The Catholic Church in the Age of Total War and Globalisation: A sprawling but intelligent history Later, Müller explores her friendship with the poet Oskar Pastior, whose experiences in a Soviet labour camp informed The Hunger Angel. Equally fascinating are the reflections on her word-collages, where language is literally cut apart and reassembled. Structured as a dialogue with her long-time editor Angelika Klammer, and beautifully translated by Kate McNaughton, the result is a sustained work of literary self-reflection. Müller reminds us how fragile freedom of thought can be. Democracies do not become authoritarian overnight. They erode through conformity, self-censorship, moral certainty and the gradual replacement of lived reality by approved narratives. Müller’s answer to ideology is attention: attention to language, memory and the irreducible particularity of human experience. This is ultimately not a book about Romania; it is about what writing protects when everything else is under threat. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.text: Figure caption, âWe will fight backâ if Russia attacks, Lithuanian PM says By Tabby Wilson Published 22 September 2026 Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked. Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams. Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Nato is thought to have several thousand troops stationed in the Baltic state, including US and German forces. Although the US is currently reviewing its deployments in Europe, Lithuanian President Gitanas NausÄda said on Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was on its way to his country. SinkeviÄius told the BBC. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly." "We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us." SinkeviÄius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year , which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally. Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons. The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons. Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops in Lithuania, but says now that it is unable to give a precise figure for the numbers stationed there. Germany - a fellow Nato ally - has pledged to send a 5,000-strong combat-ready brigade to Lithuania permanently as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. However, Nato said on Tuesday it would reach "full operational capability" by the end of 2027. The Germany military has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions. The majority of troops will be based in RÅ«dninkai, near the SuwaÅki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad. The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. "We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory." Moscow did not comment on the incident. Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine. Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel. Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members". https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/10.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate Several weeks ago, at the October 14 performance of Verdi’s masterpiece Macbeth , Metropolitan Opera General Manager Peter Gelb came out on stage to call on the audience to rise for the Ukrainian national anthem. “Ever since Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine,” declared Gelb, “the Met has stood in staunch defense of the nation’s fight for its liberty and for justice. Today, with the nation under nonstop and relentless attack, Ukraine needs our support. It needs the world’s support more than ever.” Peter Gelb [Photo by Peabody Awards / CC BY 2.0 ] This extraordinary action by the chief of the largest performing arts organization in the United States has been accompanied, in recent weeks, by a similar official declaration of support for the Ukrainian regime, prominently displayed inside the programs of various operas presented by the Met. Gelb has been in the forefront of the anti-Russian campaign ever since 2022. His statement calls Russia’s reactionary invasion, which took place more than four and a half years ago, brutal and illegal, but one word appears to be carefully omitted—“unprovoked.” The invasion was indeed provoked, and it led to the proxy war of the imperialist powers against Russia that continues to this day. This war was prepared over many years. It involved the expansion of the NATO imperialist military alliance to the borders of the former Soviet Union and the overthrow of the elected pro-Russian Ukrainian government by a fascist-backed coup in 2014. The Met issued an official statement in support of Ukraine immediately after the war began. Moreover, Gelb quickly made it a condition of employment at the Met for Russian musicians to repudiate Vladimir Putin. Anna Netrebko, one of the world’s leading sopranos and a longtime star at the Met, was fired even after she had criticized the invasion, because Gelb did not deem her statement strong enough. Although Netrebko later was awarded more than $200,000 by an arbitrator for the Met’s breach of its contract with her, Gelb stubbornly continues to denounce the soprano, saying recently that he considers her “dishonest.” The attack on Netrebko is bound up with the ethnonationalist campaign by the Kiev regime to blacken all of Russian culture, even to the extent of dropping the works of Tchaikovsky from concert programs. Netrebko’s career has continued to flourish in Europe, but she has not performed in Russia or, with the exception of one small performance in Florida, in the US. The Met has also jointly commissioned a new opera, The Mothers of Kherson , with the Polish National Opera. The new work has just premiered in Warsaw and is scheduled for performance in New York in April 2028. It is based on the story of the thousands of Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces in the early stages of the war. Of course, art can and should depict war’s crimes against children. Although no judgment can be passed on the artistic merit of this work before it is heard, it must be noted that the actions of only one side are being considered. While the Met does not typically disclose the cost of a new opera commission, composer’s and librettist’s fees plus broader development costs can easily amount to more than $1 million. The financial commitment this commission entails fits in with the Met’s propaganda campaign in support of the Zelensky regime in Kiev. The Met’s record on Ukraine is not the product of the obsession of one man. While Gelb’s wife, Canadian-Ukrainian conductor Keri-Lynn Wilson, has been very prominent in this campaign, the fundamental causes are political and not personal in nature. Gelb has acted as he has because of a broad consensus within the American ruling class in support of the proxy war, especially within the New York City financial, political and cultural establishment. A significant layer of affluent petty bourgeois like Gelb obediently follow in the ideological wake of this establishment. The nature of this consensus is clear. The aim of the war is to inflict a strategic defeat on Moscow, subordinating Russia to the status of a semi-colony, seizing its vast natural resources and consolidating US hegemony over the Eurasian landmass as preparation for war with China. While there may have been a few eyebrows raised behind the scenes about this or that detail, Gelb is clearly articulating the views of the oligarchs and the billionaires, and particularly the line of the Democratic Party, which has attacked the Trump administration from the right, for allegedly dragging its heels on this war. In this regard, it should be noted that right after the White House clash between Zelensky and Donald Trump in March 2025, the Met issued a statement praising “the heroic leader President Zelensky” and played the Ukrainian anthem before another opera performance. Ukraine gave Gelb its Order of Merit in 2023. The proxy war is not about Ukrainian “liberty” and “freedom.” That is just the window dressing designed to obscure the predatory aims of the conflict. That is the only way that the playing of the Ukrainian national anthem before a largely upper middle class and elite audience can be understood. There has been no declaration of war against Russia by the US or by the European powers, but there is a war—a de facto war—one of the fronts in the emerging third world war. Metropolitan Opera [Photo by Andreas Praefcke / CC BY 3.0 ] There are plenty of precedents for attacks on free speech and other democratic rights in the history of American capitalism in time of war or preparation for war, and musicians and other artists have not been spared. After the US entered the First World War in 1917, German music was quickly removed from concert programs. German-born conductor Karl Muck, who was well-established as the chief conductor of one of the most famous orchestras of the country, in Boston, was imprisoned on trumped-up charges for nearly 18 months before being deported. During the Korean War, and the Cold War that preceded and followed it, numerous artists, most famously the operatic bass-baritone Paul Robeson, suffered irreparable damage to their careers. The ultimatums given by Gelb to Netrebko recall the hearings of the House Un-American Activities Committee in the 1940s and 50s, as well as the demagogic anticommunism of Wisconsin Senator Joseph McCarthy. Actors, writers and other artists were told they could salvage their careers only if they recited obligatory denunciations prepared for them in advance. Gelb’s brazen and hypocritical warmongering has triggered very little criticism. There were reports that some musicians objected to turning the opera stage over to war propaganda. This was swept under the rug by instructing those protesting to simply withdraw from that section of the performance. Socialism AI by the WSWS SocialismAI.com Questions about this article? Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com Justin Davidson of New York magazine was one of the very few critics who took issue with Gelb. He ironically proposed an opera libretto based dissident Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, who was brutally killed and his body dismembered in 2018 by agents of the Saudi regime headed by de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman. Davidson suggested “a future commission” for the Met, “about a brave storyteller, gifted with eloquence and clarity, whose truths anger a vengeful king. He flees into exile, only to be entrapped and murdered just when he thought he was safe. On the Met’s stage, the writer—called, say, Jamal Khashoggi—would be sung by a heroic tenor, his tormentor by a demonic baritone.” Not only did Gelb not speak up at the time of the murder of Khashoggi, he made a deal with the murderer. As Davidson reminded his readers, “the nimbly opportunistic Peter Gelb recently struck a $100 million deal with Saudi Arabia to supply Riyadh’s new opera house with three weeks’ worth of performances each year…” The distinction made by Gelb between the brutality of Putin and that of the Saudi ruler corresponds exactly with the foreign policy of the US government. The most glaring example of Gelb’s hypocrisy is the Met’s ongoing total silence on the Israeli genocide in Gaza. In the immediate aftermath of the events of October 7, 2023, Gelb also spoke on the stage of the Met, directing the orchestra to play Verdi’s famous “Va, Pensiero,” the chorus of the Hebrew Slaves, from Nabucco . In the three years since, as 75,000 Gazans, the great majority women and children, have been slaughtered and tens of thousands of others wounded or mutilated, there have been no words from Gelb, no official pronouncements, on the stage or elsewhere. The attempt to draw an equal sign between Verdi’s music and the role of either Zionism or the cause of Ukraine in the proxy war must be answered. Verdi’s choruses were bound up with the Risorgimento , a democratic struggle to unite Italy against Austrian Habsburg domination. Using Verdi to back the imperialist proxy war, or the Zionist regime, is the exact opposite of its historic meaning and significance. Nor do Gelb’s high-flown words about liberty and suffering apply to the Iranian people subjected to months of attacks in an undeclared war, or to the Cuban people, or the hundreds of fishermen killed by US drone strikes in international waters, or the American citizens as well as legal and undocumented immigrants who have been indefinitely imprisoned or deported or even killed, as part of the endless outrages of the fascist US president. None of that gets a mention from Gelb. Ironically, while Gelb has not mentioned the war on Iran, it is this very war and its consequences that led the Saudi regime, citing economic damage, to withdraw its $100 million offer to the Met. While Gelb extols the virtues of the unelected government of Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian Trotskyist Bogdan Syrotiuk has been jailed for more than two years and has recently been sentenced to 15 years in prison for the sole “crime” of writing articles for the World Socialist Web Site opposing both Putin and Zelensky and fighting for the unity of the Russian and Ukrainian workers to put an end to the fratricidal conflict. Gelb’s actions have the odor of desperation. In the US, among broad layers of the middle class as well as the working class, there is opposition to the genocide in Gaza and to the war on Iran, and opposition to escalation of the proxy war in Ukraine. In Ukraine there is also enormous opposition, including to the forcible conscription of cannon fodder for the war. But this opposition must above all be based on the international working class, in struggle against the criminal and decaying capitalist system.
